recent_posts.title: Building a computer inside a book to explain embedded systems
recent_posts.summary: An embedded systems engineer builds a computer inside a book to practically demonstrate what an embedded system is. The project walks through the full development process: defining inputs (button, light sensor) and outputs (LED strip, e-ink display), writing firmware in C, designing a custom PCB after frying the prototype, and physically fitting everything into a hollowed-out book. Along the way, key concepts are explained: embedded systems are computers shaped for a specific purpose, distinct from general-purpose computers (which lack a fixed role) and simple electrical devices (which lack a computer entirely). The engineering process covers blinking LEDs, PWM, ADC readings, using third-party display libraries, schematic drawing, PCB layout, and hardware debugging.

recent_posts.title: How a Microcontroller starts
recent_posts.summary: Explores the complete microcontroller startup process from power-on to main() function execution. Demonstrates how ARM Cortex-M processors initialize stack pointers and program counters, set up C runtime environments, and handle memory sections. Includes hands-on implementation of custom startup code from scratch, covering interrupt vector tables, linker scripts, and C runtime initialization including data/BSS section setup.

recent_posts.title: Lessons learned from a complete embedded systems project series
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive reflection on completing a 28-video embedded systems project series covering everything from makefiles and version control to driver development, motor control, and simulation. The creator discusses lessons learned, including the benefits of bare-metal programming for education, design decisions that could have been improved (simpler mechanical design, better microcontroller choice), and the trade-offs between writing everything from scratch versus using existing libraries. Key takeaways include the importance of understanding fundamentals before using higher-level tools and the challenges of balancing educational value with practical development efficiency.

recent_posts.title: Simulation to Real-world Demo | Embedded System Project Series #27
recent_posts.summary: A developer completes the implementation of a sumo robot's state machine code, first testing it in a custom 2D simulator called BotsTD before deploying to the actual hardware. The project involves creating simulation wrappers, implementing sensor input history with ring buffers, and handling various robot states including search, attack, and retreat behaviors. The final implementation successfully demonstrates a working sumo robot that can detect opponents, avoid platform boundaries, and execute strategic movements.

recent_posts.title: How to Code a State Machine | Embedded System Project Series #26
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive tutorial on implementing state machines in C for embedded systems, demonstrated through a sumo robot project. Covers state machine design principles, creating state transition diagrams using PlantUML, and building a modular C implementation with states like wait, search, attack, and retreat. Shows practical considerations like non-blocking code execution, timer management, and memory constraints on microcontrollers.

recent_posts.title: I made a Robot 2D Simulator with C++ | Embedded System Project Series #25
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares their journey building a 2D robotics simulator from scratch using C++ to test sumo robot application code before deploying to hardware. The project combines Box2D physics engine with custom OpenGL graphics, implementing a component-based architecture with scene objects, physics simulation, and a voltage line abstraction for hardware interface compatibility. Despite the learning experience in graphics programming and software architecture, the author reflects that using existing simulators might have been more pragmatic.

recent_posts.title: How to Board Bring-up | Embedded System Project Series #24
recent_posts.summary: Board bring-up is the critical process of verifying that newly manufactured PCBs work as intended. Hardware engineers first perform electrical measurements and component checks, then software engineers flash test code to verify GPIO functionality, communication interfaces (SPI, I2C, UART), and component connections. The process involves systematic testing of each hardware component using minimal test code, with time being crucial since hardware issues require new board revisions. The demonstration shows testing LEDs, motors, sensors, and communication interfaces on a sumo robot PCB, along with build system improvements for better target management.

recent_posts.title: I2C driver in C (with VL53L0X sensor) | Embedded System Project Series #23
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive tutorial on implementing an I2C driver in C for embedded systems, specifically for interfacing with VL53L0X range sensors in a sumo robot project. The implementation covers the complete software architecture from low-level I2C communication protocol handling to higher-level sensor abstraction layers. The tutorial demonstrates proper driver layering, register-level microcontroller programming, sensor initialization, data transmission protocols, and includes practical testing with logic analyzer verification.

recent_posts.title: ADC driver with DMA in C | Embedded System Project Series #22
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive tutorial on implementing an ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter) driver with DMA functionality for a sumo robot project using MSP430 microcontroller. The implementation includes a layered architecture with ADC driver, sensor abstraction layer, and application logic to read line sensors that detect white borders on a black platform. The driver uses interrupt-driven sampling with DMA for efficient data transfer and includes practical testing with actual hardware.

recent_posts.title: Motor Control with PWM in C | Embedded System Project Series #21
recent_posts.summary: Demonstrates implementing PWM-based motor control for a robot using C on a microcontroller. Covers creating a three-layer software architecture: a PWM driver using timer peripherals, a motor driver layer for the TB6612FNG chip, and a high-level drive interface. Shows how to control brushed DC motors with variable speed and direction using pulse width modulation, including duty cycle calculations, timer configuration, and safety features like automatic motor shutdown on system assertions.
